Mammary implant pseudocapsules

One rat implant experiment reported thinner pseudocapsules and lower implant pressure after laser treatment; it did not test outcomes in people with breast implants.

Publications and records

1publication

Publication and study types

  • Controlled rat experiment1

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for reducing pseudocapsule thickness and implant pressure in rats (Palhares et al. 2009).

Summary of the Evidence

One controlled experiment studied 60 male Wistar rats with smooth silicone implants placed under the skin on the back. It was a preclinical foreign-body model, not a study of women with breast implants.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study was identified for breast-implant pseudocapsules or capsular contracture.

Animal evidence

Laser-treated rats had thinner pseudocapsules and significantly lower implant pressure than untreated animals. Histology did not show a significant overall difference between groups, apart from more swollen vessels in the treated group (Palhares et al. 2009).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used a Twin GaAlAs laser (MM Optics, Brazil) emitting continuous 780-nm near-infrared light. It irradiated four points over each implant at 1 J/cm² per pulse, in seven sessions every other day over 14 days, beginning immediately after surgery. These settings belong to the single rat protocol and do not establish an optimal human regimen.

Interpretation

The experiment found thinner capsules and lower pressure in a rat model, while most histologic features were similar. Dorsal subcutaneous implants in male rats do not reproduce breast anatomy, implant placement, or clinical contracture outcomes. The findings do not show that PBM prevents or treats capsular contracture in patients.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One controlled rat experiment found thinner pseudocapsules and lower pressure around silicone implants after laser treatment, while most tissue features were similar (Palhares et al. 2009). The model supports a possible effect on those measurements in rats, not proven prevention or treatment of human capsular contracture.
